texts.profile:
TITLE: Photosynthesis: Light Into Sugar

INTRO: Start with two easy recalls: which gas a plant takes in, and which gas it releases. Keep your answers in mind; the rule below will confirm them.

SECTION 1 - The Core Rule
Photosynthesis is the process plants use to make glucose, a sugar, from carbon dioxide and water. Light energy from the sun drives the reaction. The arrow chain shows the same idea: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen. The oxygen is released as a by-product, not the main product.
EXAMPLE: Try it: In one line, what are the two raw materials and the energy source? Answer: carbon dioxide, water, and light energy.

SECTION 2 - Where Light Is Captured
Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light. It sits inside chloroplasts, which are packed into leaf cells. So the light-capturing step happens in the chloroplasts, mainly in the leaves. A useful picture is a labelled list: leaf -> chloroplast -> chlorophyll -> light absorbed.
EXAMPLE: Try it: A comic artist uses a light box to trace a page. In a leaf, which molecule is the light-catcher? Answer: chlorophyll.

SECTION 3 - Inputs, Outputs, and the Main Site
The plant takes in carbon dioxide through small leaf openings and water through its roots. The leaf is the main factory because it holds the chloroplasts and receives sunlight. Glucose is the product the plant keeps for energy and growth. Oxygen exits as the by-product.
EXAMPLE: Try it: In a video game, a crafting recipe has inputs and outputs. Name the inputs and outputs of photosynthesis. Answer: inputs are carbon dioxide, water, and light energy; outputs are glucose and oxygen.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A leaf takes in 6 carbon dioxide molecules and 6 water molecules, with light energy. Write the products and say which is the by-product.
  1. Write the raw materials: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O.
  2. Add the energy source: light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts.
  3. Use the balanced pattern: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light energy -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2.
  4. Read the products: C6H12O6 is glucose, the sugar the plant keeps; 6 O2 is oxygen.
  5. Identify the by-product: oxygen is released, so it is the by-product.
  ANSWER: Products: glucose (C6H12O6) and oxygen (6 O2); oxygen is the by-product.

COMMON MISTAKES:
Wrong: Plants take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide during photosynthesis. Why: this swaps the gas exchange; carbon dioxide is a raw material taken in, and oxygen is the by-product released. Right: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen.

SUMMARY: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen. Chlorophyll in chloroplasts, mainly in leaves, absorbs the light. Oxygen is the by-product.

CHECK QUESTIONS:
1. A leaf has water and carbon dioxide and is kept in bright light. Which product is the sugar the plant keeps? [choices: Oxygen | Glucose | Chlorophyll | Carbon dioxide] -> Glucose
2. A leaf is given water and carbon dioxide but kept in a dark cupboard. Explain why it cannot make glucose. [typed answer] -> No light reaches the leaf, so chlorophyll cannot absorb light energy to drive the reaction.
texts.mirror:
TITLE: Photosynthesis: How a Leaf Makes Its Own Food

INTRO: A plant cannot run to the shop for a snack, so it builds its own sugar inside its leaves. The name for that job is photosynthesis. In this lesson you will learn what goes in, what powers it, what comes out, and where in the plant it happens.

SECTION 1 - The rule: a plant builds sugar from two materials
Photosynthesis is the way a plant makes its own food, a sugar called glucose. Two materials go in: carbon dioxide, a gas taken from the air, and water, pulled up by the roots. Light energy from the sun powers the change; light is energy, not a material, so it never counts as one of the ingredients. The two materials are turned into glucose, and oxygen gas comes out as a by-product, which means something made on the side. In one line the rule is: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen.
EXAMPLE: Basketball version, every step shown. Step 1: two players start the play, and here the players are carbon dioxide and water. Step 2: the coach's energy starts the play, and that is light energy; the coach is not a player, just as light is not a material. Step 3: the play scores, and the score is glucose, the plant's food. Step 4: the crowd noise comes out on the side without anyone aiming for it, and that is oxygen, the by-product.

SECTION 2 - Where it happens: leaves, chloroplasts, chlorophyll
Photosynthesis happens mainly in the leaves, because a leaf is thin and flat and catches a lot of light. Inside leaf cells are tiny green packets called chloroplasts; a cell is the smallest living unit of a plant. Chlorophyll is the green stuff inside the chloroplasts, and chlorophyll is what absorbs the light. To absorb means to take in, so chlorophyll grabs the light energy and hands it to the reaction. A plant with its leaves stripped off has almost nowhere to run photosynthesis, so it makes very little glucose.
EXAMPLE: A worked example with the last step left for you. A plant sits in a dark cupboard for two days. Step 1: check the energy source, and the rule says light energy is needed. Step 2: in the cupboard there is no light, so chlorophyll has no light energy to absorb. Step 3 is yours. Try it: with no light energy absorbed, can the leaf make glucose? Answer: no. Glucose is only built when captured light energy powers the change, so in the dark cupboard photosynthesis stops.

SECTION 3 - The chain in order
Here is the same rule as an arrow chain you can read left to right, where each arrow means leads to. Sunlight -> chlorophyll in the chloroplasts -> light energy captured -> carbon dioxide and water turned into glucose -> oxygen released. Read it backwards and you can say why a plant fails: block the sunlight, and the first arrow never fires. Leaves sit at the front of the chain, which is why they do most of the work.
EXAMPLE: Drawing-comics version, every step shown. Panel 1: a sunbeam hits a leaf, so light arrives. Panel 2: green chlorophyll inside the chloroplasts absorbs that light, so light energy is captured. Panel 3: carbon dioxide drifts in from the air and water arrives from the roots. Panel 4: the captured energy turns those two materials into glucose. Panel 5: oxygen floats away as the by-product. Try it: in Panel 2 the leaf is coloured white with a marker so it has no chlorophyll. Which panel is the first to fail? Answer: Panel 2, because nothing is there to absorb the light, so no light energy is captured and the later panels cannot happen.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A green leaf in sunlight takes in 6 molecules of carbon dioxide and 6 molecules of water. Work out how many molecules of glucose the leaf makes, and how many molecules of oxygen it releases. A molecule is a tiny particle of a substance.
  1. List the materials going in: carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil. The leaf has 6 carbon dioxide and 6 water.
  2. Note the energy: sunlight, absorbed by chlorophyll. Light is energy, not a material, so it stays out of the ingredient tally.
  3. Find the glucose. One glucose molecule holds 6 carbon atoms, and the 6 carbon dioxide molecules supply 6 carbon atoms between them, so the leaf can build exactly 1 glucose molecule.
  4. Count the oxygen atoms going in: 6 carbon dioxide hold 6 x 2 = 12 oxygen atoms, and 6 water hold 6 x 1 = 6 oxygen atoms, so 12 + 6 = 18 oxygen atoms in total.
  5. Take out the oxygen that stays inside the glucose: 1 glucose holds 6 oxygen atoms, so 18 - 6 = 12 oxygen atoms are left over.
  6. Pair the leftovers into oxygen gas. Oxygen gas travels in pairs, so 12 oxygen atoms make 12 / 2 = 6 molecules of oxygen gas.
  7. Check the tally: 6 carbon dioxide + 6 water -> 1 glucose + 6 oxygen. Carbon: 6 in and 6 in the glucose. Hydrogen: 12 in the water and 12 in the glucose. Oxygen: 18 in and 6 + 12 = 18 out. Everything balances.
  ANSWER: The leaf makes 1 molecule of glucose and releases 6 molecules of oxygen as the by-product.

COMMON MISTAKES:
Wrong: Plants get their food from the soil, so photosynthesis starts in the roots. Why: this skips the rule that the plant builds its own sugar; the soil supplies water, not glucose, and the sugar is made in the leaf. Right: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen, with chlorophyll in the leaf chloroplasts absorbing the light.
Wrong: The plant takes in oxygen for photosynthesis and gives out carbon dioxide. Why: the two gases are swapped round; carbon dioxide is the material going in and oxygen is the by-product coming out. Right: carbon dioxide goes in, oxygen comes out: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen.
Wrong: 6 carbon dioxide + 6 water makes 6 glucose and 1 oxygen. Why: the counts are the wrong way round, because 6 carbon dioxide only holds 6 carbon atoms and each glucose needs 6, so there is enough for just 1 glucose. Right: 6 carbon dioxide + 6 water makes 1 glucose and 6 oxygen, which balances.

SUMMARY: Photosynthesis is a plant building glucose from carbon dioxide and water, powered by light energy from the sun. Chlorophyll inside the chloroplasts of leaf cells absorbs that light, and oxygen leaves as the by-product. The one-line rule to remember: carbon dioxide + water + light energy -> glucose + oxygen, mainly in the leaves.

CHECK QUESTIONS:
1. Which pair of materials does a plant turn into glucose? Hint: one drifts in from the air and one is pulled up from the soil. [choices: Oxygen and sunlight | Carbon dioxide and water | Water and glucose | Glucose and oxygen] -> Carbon dioxide and water
2. A leaf is sealed in a clear, sunlit jar with plenty of water in its stem, but every trace of carbon dioxide is removed from the jar. Can the leaf still make glucose? Say why. Hint: check each of the two materials against what the jar provides. [typed answer] -> No. Carbon dioxide is one of the two materials that get turned into glucose, and it has been removed, so the reaction cannot run.
3. A leaf has one white patch with no chlorophyll in it. Sunlight, water and carbon dioxide all reach the patch. Explain whether the patch can make glucose, and name the step of the chain that fails. Hint: run the chain in order, sunlight first, then ask what absorbs it. [typed answer] -> No. Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts is what absorbs the light, so with no chlorophyll the light energy is never absorbed and no glucose is made in the patch.
